item.title: Marked INAR model and the rough Hawkes--Heston limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.29565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a discrete-time Monte Carlo algorithm for the rough Hawkes-Heston model based on a nearly unstable marked integer-valued autoregressive (INAR) process. We implement the algorithm with a block fast Fourier transform (FFT) scheme that evaluates the excitation convolution in $O(N\log^2 N)$ operations per path on an $N$-bin grid. We prove joint convergence in law of the spot variance, log price and common marked point measure to their rough Hawkes-Heston limits. We prove convergence of European call and put option prices, as well as convergence of arithmetic Asian and down-and-out put option prices to their continuously monitored values. For European options, the one-year implied volatility smiles computed from the grid transform approach the continuous affine reference across four roughness levels. Monte Carlo experiments on the same three grids compare arithmetic Asian and down-and-out put option prices with a finer-grid reference and demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Wang, Yingli Wang, Lingjiong Zhu

item.title: Wasserstein Penalisation as an Endogenous Breadth Constraint in Penalised Mean-Variance Portfolio Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.30046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A manager who wants a long-only book and has read that Wasserstein-robust mean-variance selection improves risk-adjusted performance faces two decisions: how much robustness to buy, and how diversified to be. In the long-only problem, and for the penalised scalarisation of the robust objective, these are the same decision: the robustification term depends on the weight vector alone, so on the simplex the radius prices effective breadth and nothing else. The equivalence is specific to that scalarisation; it fails for the return-floored form, where the radius also raises the return threshold, and for the exact robust risk-minimisation problem. Two consequences follow. First, a negative one needing no alpha: positive definiteness of the covariance does not imply breadth, since no bound on the dispersion of the mean and no positive spectral floor prevents the long-only optimum from collapsing onto a single asset, so the breadth of the minimum-variance benchmark is an irreducible input. Second, identification: matched to a benchmark with the same effective number of holdings, the robust portfolio attains the same mean-variance value to solver precision, so the radius carries no in-sample information beyond breadth selection, and the residual weight difference lives in near-null directions of the covariance. On fourteen A-share panels the ex post comparison is exact by construction, hence no evidence. The informative test fixes breadth before the window is used: a cap set to the historical level of the robust portfolio's realised breadth recovers about five sixths of its gain, leaving a residual of seven to eleven basis points per day across five tracking rules, whereas a fixed target recovers only a quarter to two fifths. The robust portfolio is thus a breadth rule, not a fixed breadth choice. We close with a reporting standard that makes the attribution checkable.
item.dc:creator: Jiahao Chen

item.title: CCFinance: Reconstructing Financial News Samples from Web Archives
item.description: arXiv:2611.30737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proprietary news archives assign stories to firms, so reproducing a financial study often requires access to both the articles and the vendor's assignments. CCFinance lets researchers reconstruct firm coverage under different selection rules by recording which version of a story was captured, which issuers it names and how often each appears. From 14.8 million English-language records in Fine News, derived from public Common Crawl News, we identify 5.22 million distinct, consistently dated articles with issuer links. Exact reconstruction requires the restricted snapshot and derived artifacts. We compare GLiNER and Stanza on 250 model-labeled article leads and assess issuer links and story focus against blinded model judgments. Estimated precision among 475 accepted links is 96.8%. Among held-out articles with a detected company, requiring three mentions raises subject precision from 31.9% to 66.1%. Across the 2017-2025 panel, the same rule reduces the number of issuer-years with at least 50 qualifying stories from 13,918 to 8,641. Three reimplementations examine volatility tracking, bank networks and overnight returns. In the network study, bank pairs appearing together rose from 177 to 242 across publishers between January and April 2020, but fell from 50 to 35 within Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Marcus Gawronsky

item.title: Critical step size of stochastic gradient descent for a linear neuron: an exact solution and the role of the input spectrum
item.description: arXiv:2611.30880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online stochastic gradient descent for a single linear neuron in a teacher-student setting with Gaussian inputs of arbitrary covariance. The mean-square errors of the $N$ weights obey a closed linear recursion of dimension $N$, which we solve exactly. We prove that the dynamics converges if and only if the step size is below a critical value $\lambda_c$, given by an explicit scalar equation that involves all the eigenvalues of the input covariance, and we obtain the stationary error of each weight, which diverges at $\lambda_c$. This condition coincides with the classical mean-square stability condition of the least-mean-squares filter; our derivation is elementary and self-contained. We then show that $\lambda_c$ is controlled by the effective rank $\Omega_1$ of the input covariance rather than by the number of parameters, $1/(\Omega_1+2) \leq \lambda_c < 1/\Omega_1$ in rescaled units: the critical step size is inversely proportional to $N$ only for isotropic inputs, whereas it decays more slowly, or saturates, for power-law spectra. Finally, we extend the solution to mini-batches of size $B$: the critical step size grows linearly with $B$ and saturates once $B$ exceeds the effective rank.
item.dc:creator: S\'ebastien Valeyre

item.title: Design an Algorithmic Stablecoin based on a Predictive PID Controller
item.description: arXiv:2611.30982v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cryptocurrencies issued based on blockchain technology have attracted increasing attention in recent years. However, their high volatility makes it difficult for them to become circulating currencies. This led to the creation of stablecoins. Existing stablecoins can be divided into three main categories: stablecoins pegged to fiat currencies, stablecoins collateralized by crypto assets, and algorithmically controlled stablecoins. Most existing stablecoins are either of the first two types. We design an algorithmic stablecoin controlled only by a predictive Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller, which uses the price forecasted by Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model as part of its input. Simulation experiments show that, under ideal market conditions, the stablecoin can achieve long-term goals that fluctuate within a pre-defined range. Furthermore, it consistently restores prices to the anchor interval in the presence of exogenous disturbances.
item.dc:creator: Yuqiao Zhao, Wai-Ki Ching, Chi-Wing Wong

item.title: Gated Payoff-Weighted Net Profit Maximization For Online Portfolio Selection With Transaction Costs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29552v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we study online portfolio selection (OLPS) problems. The net profit maximization (NPM) acting upon Adaptive Online Moving Average (AOLMA), namely the AOLNPM strategy in portfolio selection, trades when forecast gain exceeds the transaction cost. In essence, this method relies heavily on calibrated forecasts. Indeed, we show that AOLMA forecasts overstate the realized relative returns. We therefore design a gate that adjusts how strongly an AOLMA forecast is used; for each asset, it learns the recent mixture proportion assigned to AOLMA from predictive likelihoods against a neutral forecast (no change). The proportion therefore estimates the extent to which the forecast is realized. We then feed the resulting forecast into the NPM portfolio rule, where the gate acts as an asset-specific cost threshold. A payoff-weighted fund combines gated NPM experts with fixed decay factors in proportion to their wealth and needs no learning rate. On nine datasets with a transaction cost rate of 0.1%, our method produces 5.9 times the wealth of AOLNPM in geometric mean and sits above AOLNPM on every dataset, with its preponderance growing with the cost rate.
item.dc:creator: Grace Chengrong Xie, Alvey Qianli Lin, Wai Ki Ching

item.title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
item.description: arXiv:2611.31190v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-\delta$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($\delta=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.
item.dc:creator: Avinash Kumar Singh, Bhaskarjit Sarmah, Stefano Pasquali
